outcomes: Convert a linear score into a probability with sigmoid
Derive binary cross-entropy from Bernoulli likelihood
Compute stable loss directly from logits
Train and threshold a binary logistic classifier

probability.name: Probability
probability.definition: A number from zero to one representing uncertainty about an event.
probability.explanation: In a binary classifier, the model outputs a conditional probability estimate for the positive class given an input. Zero and one are the endpoints; 0.5 represents equal modeled odds. A probability is not yet a decision. A threshold converts it into a predicted class, and different applications can choose different thresholds. Model probabilities can also be poorly calibrated, so a value such as 0.8 should not be trusted as an observed 80 percent frequency without separate evaluation.

logit.name: Logit
logit.definition: An unrestricted model score converted to probability by sigmoid or softmax.
logit.explanation: Binary logistic regression computes z = w dot x + b, then applies sigmoid. In that binary setting z is the log-odds, and positive z implies probability above one half. A multiclass model instead supplies one logit per class to softmax; only relative scores determine probabilities, so one positive score need not imply probability above one half. Retaining logits allows stable cross-entropy without taking logarithms of rounded probabilities.

sigmoid.name: Sigmoid
sigmoid.definition: The function 1 divided by 1 plus exp of the negative input.
sigmoid.explanation: Sigmoid maps every finite real logit into the interval from zero to one. At zero it returns one half, and increasing the logit increases the probability smoothly. Its derivative is p(1−p), which helps simplify logistic-regression gradients. Direct evaluation can overflow for a very negative logit, so the Rust implementation uses separate positive and negative branches. This numerical rearrangement preserves the mathematics while keeping intermediate exponentials bounded.

likelihood.name: Likelihood
likelihood.definition: The probability assigned to observed targets, viewed as a function of model parameters.
likelihood.explanation: For an example with binary target y, a model assigning positive-class probability p gives the observed target probability p when y is one and 1−p when y is zero. Assuming examples contribute independently, likelihood multiplies these terms. Products of many small values underflow, so optimization uses the negative log-likelihood, turning products into sums. Minimizing binary cross-entropy is therefore the same parameter objective as maximizing Bernoulli likelihood under the model assumptions.

binary-cross-entropy.name: Binary cross-entropy
binary-cross-entropy.definition: The negative log-likelihood loss for a binary target.
binary-cross-entropy.explanation: For target y and probability p, binary cross-entropy is −[y log p + (1−y) log(1−p)]. It strongly penalizes confident wrong predictions. Computing this expression from a probability that rounded to zero or one can produce infinities. The equivalent logits formula max(z,0) − zy + log(1 + exp(−|z|)) remains finite for large finite logits. The chapter averages this loss over examples and states that reduction explicitly.

checks: BCE at logit zero equals ln 2
Stable BCE remains finite at logits plus and minus 1000
Analytical gradients match central differences on the stable logits objective
Every fixture point is classified correctly at threshold 0.5
limitations: Training accuracy on separable synthetic points does not establish calibration
The project covers binary rather than multiclass classification
A 0.5 threshold is illustrative and must be chosen from application costs
